title: [3.x] Add `GDScript` optimizer
body:
Optimization via Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)

* Inline functions
* Loop invariant code motion (LICM)
* Loop unrolling
* Unused expression elimination
* Constant Folding

Implements https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3760
Implements some of https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11490
Partially supports https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7375

Optimization is currently **off** by default, and must be switched on via `project_settings/application/run/gdscript_optimization`. Precise settings can be selected per gdscript file.

_(There is code to activate it on a file by file basis, only where one of the new keywords are used, however, now the optimizer offers LICM, unused expression elimination and constant folding, these are generally useful, so make sense to be in use whenever optimization is on.)_

Changes to existing engine code are minimal, so the existing parser etc remain easy to understand and the complexity is kept low. Most of the new code is enclosed within `gdscript_optimizer` and `gdscript_reconstructor`.

Could likely be ported to 4.x if desired (as it is fairly self contained), at least as a stop gap. From discussions on rocket chat, 4.x GDScript maintainers may have other grander plans there.

## Background
I normally don't touch GDScript, but I was profiling GDScript a couple of weeks ago with a view to optimizing anything obvious, and saw that function calls were pretty slow (other people have previously noticed this as a bottleneck).

So for fun I decided to have a go at inlining via altering the GDScript source.

First go I wrote a new parser (independent of the existing one) and successfully got inlining working. After some discussions, it was clear it would be far more robust to bandit the existing parser (which deals with all esoteric cases), so I spent some time figuring out how it worked. Once I had some basic inlining working I added some more features.

## Inlining

![simple](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/55509e86-e37f-41f4-b124-04bfb8ca7c2c)

On advice from vnen and other contributors it became clear that inlining functions automatically was problematic, because in gdscript functions are virtual by default, so we could easily end up inlining a local function that might be replaced by a function in another script at runtime.

For this reason I added an `inline` keyword (e.g. `inline func myfunc()`), which has two purposes:

1) signals explicitly to the optimizer that you want a function inlined
2) allows the system to explicitly disallow calling virtual functions with the same name

In some cases, there are situations in which a function cannot be inlined, and (1) enables the optimizer to log messages to this effect and the reason. (2) prevents the user from shooting themselves in the foot, by producing error messages when the user tries to use an `inline` function as virtual.

In terms of implementation there were some complications, particularly there is no jump instruction in GDScript, which makes implementing early return statements slightly more complex. However in most cases these are handled well, in exceptional cases the inline cannot be performed and it will emit a warning to this effect and the reason.

During the inlining process, local variables are renamed with unique names (using `__` as a prefix and unique ID as a postfix) to prevent naming conflicts. It is assumed that the `__` prefix is not allowed by users (this is a standard used in c++ so it seemed reasonable). Unused parameters are removed, constant parameters are passed as constants (and so can be folded).

UPDATE: Inlining is now supported for functions within nested classes. This is super useful for utility classes (e.g. basic types) that can now have inlined accessors etc.

## Loop invariant code motion (LICM)

After inlining it is common to have variables from the inline in the loop which could be better declared or assigned outside the loop. LICM will attempt to move these variables outside the loop where possible (where no side effects are detected).

LICM currently covers:
* moving variable declarations outside the loop
* moving expressions (that are invariant) outside the loop, especially math expressions 

Moving heavy math outside the loop can be a big win in some situations.

![licm](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a5ef9f8d-e735-4607-83f4-0e8a1b6f8ca1)

## Loop unrolling
In tight for loops, the actual machinery of the for loop itself can become a bottleneck. Loop unrolling is a common optimization. Here we determine the length of the loop, which determines whether a loop should be unrolled, and how many unrolls should be done in a `unit`. The actual unroll consists of pre-calculating the number of units (e.g. 8), running a loop for the units, then a loop for the leftovers.

This falls back to an unrolled loop if the iterator isn't compatible.

Because there are a number of situations where you wouldn't want unrolling (e.g. small numbers of iterations that wouldn't benefit, non-compatible iterations), unrolling must be requested with a new `unroll` keyword.

```
unroll for i in range (100):
	do_stuff()
```
As with inlining, there are some situations in which unrolling is determined not possible, in which case it will output a warning and reason.

## Unused expression elimination
This is fairly limited for now but does work for the case of `const` values. This is extremely useful for debugging, you can e.g.:
```
const debugging = false

if debugging:
	for i in range (100):
		print("some stuff")

```
This whole section will be removed when `debugging` is set as false. The only caveat is that it *must* be a `const` in order to work.

UPDATE: This can now evaluate a lot of const expressions to eliminate dead code. For instance, `if my_const == 5` can now be evaluated.

## Constant folding
* math expressions that use constants can now often be folded (optimized out) at compile time
* this includes numbers hard coded in the script, _and_ constants defined e.g. at class scope
* inline function parameters passed as constant can also be folded, entire inline functions can be evaluated at compile time

## Example

<details>

### Original source
```
extends Node2D

inline func myfunc(chicken : int):
	return 2 + chicken

func _ready():
	var total = 0
	
	unroll for n in range (1024):
		total += myfunc(9)
	
	print(str(total))

```

### Observations
* the `(2 + __chicken0)` expression is calculated once outside the loop and reused
* the unroll has to check the counter is an `int` (only technique supported), and must be currently checked at runtime
* the counter is not kept in sync in this example, but if required it will automatically sync a counter to call functions etc.

### Still to do
* the 8 identical expressions can be merged into one operation
* 1024 is a const, so some branches could be eliminated (it assumes non-const for now, which is worst case)

However I didn't want to get too carried away (no point unless we proceed with this). :slightly_smiling_face: 

</details>

## Logging and Options
Options are provided in ProjectSettings:
* global on / off switch for optimization (in `application/run/gdscript_optimization`)
* logging level from 0 (none) to 5 (full) (in `debug/gdscript/optimization/logging_level`)

And each script can now individually turn on / off optimization and options:

![script_options](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5d5f1a6b-064d-4831-b4fd-e52c7386650c)

Logs can show for each optimization a before and after of the affected code, so the user can confirm the optimization is working as intended. For this, there is a `Reconstructor` class which can do a basic reconstruction estimation of `GDScript` back from an AST tree. Additionally there is the ability to print AST trees directly, which provides even more information.

![ast](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/01f4ec4c-c634-4a4c-a366-44432bb82bfd)

## Performance
It is important to realize that GDScript optimization is only useful and worth doing on GDScript bottlenecks. If you are not stressing GDScript, then you will see little benefit. This is not a magic wand that will make all games faster.

That said, for bottleneck areas, increases in speed of 5x or more are possible. Users are encouraged to try it out.

#### Example 1:
```
extends Node2D

inline func myfunc(chicken, duck):
	return chicken + ((duck * 2) - (duck / 2) + 2 / 2)

func _ready():
	var before = OS.get_ticks_msec()
	var total = 0
	
	for n in range (1024 * 1024 * 10):
		total += myfunc(1, 9) + myfunc(2, 2) - myfunc(2, 2) - myfunc(2, 2)
	
	var after = OS.get_ticks_msec()
	print("Took " + str(after - before) + "ms.")
	print(str(total))
```
_becomes_
```
func _ready():
	var before = OS.get_ticks_msec()
	var total = 0
	var __temp_0 = 14 - (9 / 2)
	for n in range (10485760):
		total += __temp_0
	
	var after = OS.get_ticks_msec()
	print((("Took " + str((after - before))) + "ms."))
	print(str(total))
```
_before_ 7491ms
_after_ 377ms (20x faster)
_after with unroll_ 221ms (34x faster)

#### Example 2:
Same as above but main line becomes:
```
	for n in range (1024 * 1024 * 10):
		total += myfunc(n, 9) + myfunc(2, 2) - myfunc(2, 2) - myfunc(2, 2)
```
This means the first expression can't be combined with the others.

_before_ 7531ms
_after_ 818ms (9x faster)
_unrolling is not faster in this case_

## Debugging GDScript
There is one area of which users must be aware - as is the case in most languages, optimized code is much harder to step through and debug.

Stepping through *is* supported, although the line numbers may not directly correspond with the original source in optimized areas (it uses some logic to decide on line numbers, which could no doubt be improved).

For this reason it is recommended that you switch off optimization in regular development, then switch it on just to test bottlenecks, and for the final export.

## Bugs
In the case of regressions, as well as reporting bugs, users can:
* turn off optimization via project settings (overkill, but this will always work :slightly_smiling_face: )
* switch off the relevant optimization per script (or turn off optimization for problem script)

## Testing
Tested so far in:
* Trucktown
* 3D platformer
* Jetpaca
* TPS Shooter
* WroughtFlesh

Compiler optimization is something that is notorious for regressions and requiring a lot of testing. A lot of my dev time has been spent identifying and fixing before / after regressions. This is the same for clang and GCC guys.

For testing I have often turned off the requirement for the `inline` and `unroll` keywords (these can be switched off in `gdscript_optimizer.cpp` at the top) which is handy for letting it go crazy on existing code to find bugs, although in the case of `inline` this type of testing requires some care because it can throw up false positives for virtual functions.

Longterm, it would be nice to add some general test cases to CI for the optimizer, which can check for correctness of results (I've been doing this manually so far for each situation). I'm not super familiar with the testing framework in 3.x so that will take some research.

It is fully expected that there will be a few problematic cases I haven't come across yet, but the ability to turn on and off inlining / unrolling per function, and the switches per gdscript file makes it fairly easy to deal with / report on github.

## Notes
* Godot 4.x seems to be moving over to annotations (e.g. `@abstract`) instead of keywords for some things.
We don't have annotations in 3.x afaik, but we could easily make the keywords e.g. `@inline` for consistency if preferred. (otoh any 3.x to 4.x script converters could do this job too).
* It would be relatively easy to add support to 3.6 / 3.5 for loading and ignoring these keywords, in order to allow loading 3.7 scripts in 3.5 / 3.6 with minimum fuss.
* I've added terminal colors for pretty printing to consoles.
* I've also added the ability for Godot IDE to support terminal colors (this could be used for other editor features).
* Other than recognised codes, `EditorLog` eats ANSI character codes (I adapted this from 4.x).

![syntax_coloring](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2984987c-5958-4cae-ba37-44dd336eb800)

## Discussion

### On / off switch
Currently optimization global switch is in project settings, and there are no specific settings in the `export` section.

This is of course super flexible, as you may wish to run in the editor with / without optimization, and also export with or without optimization. However in the longterm we may decide to have the ability to have an export setting that can override the project setting, making it easier to make e.g. a debug / release export without having to manually worry about the project setting being correct for your export. e.g. `optimization - default (from proj setting), off, on`, something like that.

### Dead code elimination for e.g. debug / release builds / os
Currently constants for dead code elimination must be set up manually. There is some interest in being able to switch this at compile time for things like `OS.is_debug_build`, `OS.has_feature` and other similar functions. This could probably be added as a follow up.

i.e. currently for dead code elimination you need e.g.
```
const IS_DEBUG = true
```
whereas this will work but won't be optimized:
```
const IS_DEBUG = OS.is_debug_build
```

### Optimization at export / runtime
Currently optimization is done at runtime, even in exports. The export is stored as bytecode so has a slightly different `reload` but the functionality is similar. This could potentially be moved to export time, although this may have some conflicts with the ability to do dead code elimination for features depending on the platform (maybe this is a trade off we would be happy to make, or we can offer a second optimization step for dead code elimination only at runtime).

Optimization is reasonably fast, but could potentially slow level loading a little if a game had a lot of scripts, and this could be avoided by ahead of time optimization.

Doing ahead of time would entail an extra (potentially error prone) step, which would be regenerating source code from the optimized AST. This is already done to an extent for debugging / logging, however making it robust and bug free would take some effort. For this reason I have not attempted this in this PR and left as a potential follow up feature.

### Godot 3.x / 4.x GDScript differences

It is clear some of the GDScript maintainers are also exploring other avenues:
* add optimizations at the level of CFG (control flow graph) rather than AST
* converting to SSA form (static single assignment) - this makes some optimizations easier
* compile directly from optimized (our side) to assembly language or WASM or similar
* compile to intermediate of some sort, then run the intermediate through a regular compiler (with in built optimizations)

I'm of the opinion that there's been no significant optimization here (afaik) for the 7 years I've been working on Godot 3, so I'm slightly sceptical of waiting for the perfect solution - "perfect is the enemy of good enough". :thinking: 

And if we later come up with better ways, we can replace existing systems (providing the API is the same, and it seems at least an `inline` keyword will be needed).

Although there may be plans for more elaborate methods in Godot 4, in Godot 3 I don't think it seems likely that anything major will be backported (like compilation to assembly), so making best use of what we have is more important (also has least potential for regressions).
